titleText.es: Supongo que si ella aceptara las realidades irracionales, difícilmente estaría en mis fantasías.
titleText.en: I guess if she accepted irrational realities, she'd hardly be my fantasy.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: there were; there existed, in an unreal or wished-for situation
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hubiera is a special form of haber used when existence is imagined rather than presented as fact. After si, it often introduces a wish or an unreal condition.

example.en: If only there were a solution!

cardDefinitions.answerEn: any; some possible
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With an imagined or uncertain possibility, alguna can have the natural English sense “any.” It is feminine because it describes a feminine noun, such as idea or manera.

example.en: Is there any way out?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; links manera to the result it would make possible
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In una manera de que..., de joins “a way” to a clause describing what that way would allow.

example.es: Buscamos una manera de que todos participen.
example.en: We are looking for a way for everyone to participate.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: we could; we might be able to, in an imagined situation
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Pudiéramos is a special form of poder used for a hypothetical possibility involving “we.” Compare podemos, “we can,” for a possibility presented as real now.

example.en: I wish we could stay.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: together
to; in being, after tener suerte
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tener suerte uses de before the action or circumstance that is fortunate.

example.en: I am lucky to live here.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to have each other; to have us
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The action word tener means “to have.” The attached nos normally means “us”; when the same two or more people both do and receive the action, context gives it the reciprocal sense “each other.”

example.en: It is good to have each other nearby.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: part of a todo esto: by the way; speaking of that
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This a belongs to the fixed transition a todo esto rather than marking a destination.

example.en: By the way, what time is it?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: part of a todo esto: by the way; speaking of that
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Inside this fixed transition, todo does not simply mean “all” on its own.

example.en: By the way, what time is it?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: part of a todo esto: by the way; speaking of that
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Inside this fixed transition, esto points back loosely to the topic before introducing a related thought.

example.en: By the way, what time is it?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: it started; it began
I remember
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is a present form of recordar. With no before it, no recuerdo means “I don't remember.”

example.en: I remember her name.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: we ended up; we finished in a resulting state
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Acabamos can mean “we finish,” but followed directly by a word describing a state, it tells the final condition that resulted.

example.en: We ended up exhausted.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to imagine it
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Imaginar is the unchanged dictionary form “to imagine.” The attached lo means “it” and names what is being imagined.

example.en: I can't imagine it.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: happening
really does; indeed, as part of sí que
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The accent distinguishes affirmative sí from conditional si, “if.” Before que and a changed verb, sí adds strong confirmation rather than answering a yes-or-no question by itself.

example.en: Ana really does work a lot.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: part of sí que, which strongly confirms what follows
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In this pattern, que works with sí to add emphasis; it does not introduce an English “that” clause.

example.en: That really does help.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: puts; subjects, as part of poner a prueba
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Pone is a form of poner. In poner a prueba, the expression means to test someone or something.

example.es: El viaje pone a prueba su paciencia.
example.en: The trip tests her patience.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: part of poner a prueba: to test
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In the fixed expression poner a prueba, a has no useful separate English translation.

example.es: La pregunta me pone a prueba.
example.en: The question tests me.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: test; part of poner a prueba, to test
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Prueba is “test,” and with poner a it forms the conventional expression poner a prueba.

example.es: La pregunta me pone a prueba.
example.en: The question tests me.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: limits; boundaries
fantasy; imagined scenario
that, in the reaction eso es: that's it
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Eso normally points to an idea or thing as “that.” In the reaction eso es, it identifies an explanation or answer as the right one.

example.en: “The blue key?” “That's it!”

cardDefinitions.answerEn: is, in the reaction eso es: that's it
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This form of ser combines with eso in a conventional reaction that recognizes the answer or realization.

example.en: “The blue key?” “That's it!”

cardDefinitions.answerEn: only; sole
explanation
temporary; fleeting
we will disappear
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The ending -emos added to desaparecer marks a future action by “we.”

example.en: We will disappear before dawn.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: it ends; it finishes, referring to a future event after en cuanto
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Termine is a special form of terminar used because the ending has not happened yet. Spanish commonly uses this form after en cuanto when looking forward to a future event.

example.en: I will leave as soon as it ends.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I will lose
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The ending -é added to perder marks a future action by “I.”

example.en: I will miss the train.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: you will lose
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The ending -ás added to perder marks a future action by informal singular “you.”

example.en: You will lose the opportunity.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: myself; marks irse, to leave
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With a form of ir, me can mark irse, which can mean “to leave” rather than simply “to go.”

example.en: I am going to leave soon.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to leave (as part of irse)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Ir normally means “to go.” With a matching small pronoun, as in me voy a ir or nos vamos a ir, it can express leaving.

example.en: We are going to leave early.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to burn
fucking; damned, a vulgar intensifier
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Before a noun, puto can add strong anger or contempt rather than describing a literal property. It is offensive or very informal, so avoid it in polite settings.

example.en: Turn off that fucking noise!

cardDefinitions.answerEn: burn; an informal command to one person
cardDefinitions.noteEn: For the affirmative informal command of a regular -ar verb, use the same form as the ordinary él/ella present: quemar becomes quema.

example.en: Burn the letter.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: fire
I will clean; I will cleanse
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The ending -é added to limpiar marks a future action by “I.” In a dramatic context, clean can carry the stronger sense “cleanse.”

example.en: I will clean the kitchen tomorrow.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: demonic; devilish

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can you begin a wish about a situation that is not real now?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use si followed by a special past-looking verb form such as tuviera or hubiera.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Si means “if.” For an unreal present wish, the next verb takes a form often ending in -ra: tener becomes tuviera, and haber becomes hubiera. This form is called the imperfect subjunctive; in this use it marks the situation as imagined, not a claim about the past. The wish can stand alone as an exclamation.

example.en: If only I had more time!

cardDefinitions.promptEs: una manera de que alguien haga algo
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you describe a way that would let someone do something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use una manera de que, then name the person and put their action in the special form used for a desired or merely possible result.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Manera names the way, and de que introduces the result it would make possible. When that result is wanted, searched for, or hypothetical rather than stated as a fact, Spanish changes the action verb: participan becomes participen, and pueden becomes puedan. This special form is called the subjunctive.

example.es: Buscamos una manera de que todos participen.
example.en: We are looking for a way for everyone to participate.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone is lucky to do or have something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching form of tener, then suerte de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tener changes to match the lucky person: tengo suerte, tienes suerte, tenemos suerte. De connects that good fortune to the action. The following action stays in its dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as vivir.

example.en: We are lucky to live here.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you make it explicit that two people do something to each other?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use el uno al otro for two masculine people or a mixed pair; change the endings when the people are feminine.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The expression literally pairs “the one” with “the other.” Use la una a la otra for two feminine people. It often appears with nos, se, or another small object word when the verb needs one.

example.es: Nos ayudamos el uno al otro.
example.en: We help each other.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What does a todo esto do when someone changes or reconnects the topic?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: It means “by the way,” “speaking of that,” or “after all that.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Speakers use a todo esto to introduce a thought prompted by what came before, often a question that has just occurred to them. Its meaning comes from the whole expression, not by translating its three words separately.

example.es: A todo esto, ¿cuándo empieza la reunión?
example.en: By the way, when does the meeting start?

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something ended up in a particular state?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching form of acabar followed directly by a word that describes the final state.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Acabar often means “to finish.” Without de and followed by a state word, it can instead describe the condition that resulted: acabó vacío means it ended up empty. The state word changes for gender and number when it is an adjective: vacía, vacíos, or vacías.

example.en: The box ended up empty.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you evaluate an action as easy, difficult, important, or similar?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use es, then the describing word, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Es presents a general judgment, such as es fácil or es difícil. The action being judged stays in its dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir: aprender, salir, imaginar. There is no separate “it” before es in Spanish.

example.en: It is easy to learn with practice.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you strongly confirm that something really is true?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put sí que before the changed verb to mean “really does,” “certainly is,” or “indeed.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The accent on sí matters: sí confirms, while si without an accent means “if.” Que is part of this emphatic pattern and does not need a separate “that” in English. The following verb still changes normally for the person and time.

example.en: Marta really does know how to cook.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: poner algo o a alguien a prueba
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something tests a person, ability, or limit?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching form of poner, name what is tested, and add a prueba; the position of the tested item can vary.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Poner is literally “to put,” but poner a prueba is the conventional expression “to test” or “to put to the test.” With a person, Spanish normally marks that person with a: poner a Marta a prueba. With a thing, the thing can follow poner directly.

example.es: Este problema pone a prueba nuestra paciencia.
example.en: This problem tests our patience.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What can you say when you suddenly recognize the right answer or explanation?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Say ¡Eso es! to mean “That's it!” or “Exactly!”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This short reaction confirms that the idea just mentioned is the answer. It is more idiomatic than translating eso and es separately in this use.

example.en: “The blue door?” “That's it!”

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that one future action will happen as soon as another one happens?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a future statement, then en cuanto and a special form of the action that has not happened yet.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: En cuanto means “as soon as.” When the event after it is still in the future, Spanish uses a special verb form called the subjunctive: llega becomes llegue, and termina becomes termine. The other clause can use the future, as in llamaré, to say what will happen then. For a habitual fact, use the ordinary present instead.

example.en: I will call you as soon as I arrive.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say “to make noise” in Spanish?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacer followed by ruido.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish conventionally pairs hacer, “to make or do,” with ruido, “noise.” Hacer changes for the person and time: hago ruido, hacen ruido, hizo ruido.

example.en: The neighbors make a lot of noise.

regions.labelEs: SI HUBIERA ALGUNA MANERA DE QUE PUDIÉRAMOS ESTAR JUNTOS.

applications.explanationEn: Si introduces the wished-for situation, and hubiera presents existence as imagined rather than real.

applications.exampleEs: MANERA DE QUE PUDIÉRAMOS ESTAR JUNTOS
applications.explanationEn: Manera de que introduces the result the imagined way would permit; pudiéramos marks that ability as hypothetical, and estar juntos supplies the possible action and state.

regions.labelEs: TENEMOS TANTA SUERTE DE TENERNOS EL UNO AL OTRO. A TODO ESTO, ¿CÓMO EMPEZÓ?

applications.explanationEn: Tenemos identifies the fortunate people, suerte names the good fortune, and de connects it to tenernos, whose action stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Nos is attached to the end of tener, the unchanged -er form, and supplies the people received by the action.
The full four-word expression makes the reciprocal relationship between the two people explicit.
The three words form a transition that reconnects the conversation before the following question.

regions.labelEs: NO, EN SERIO, ¿CÓMO ACABAMOS JUNTOS? ES DIFÍCIL IMAGINARLO SUCEDIENDO.

applications.explanationEn: En and serio form the fixed conversational expression that signals a sincere, non-joking question.
Acabamos names the resulting outcome for “we,” and juntos is the state in which they ended up.
Es difícil supplies the general judgment, while imaginarlo is the unchanged -ar action being judged.
Lo is attached to imaginar, the unchanged -ar form, and supplies the thing imagined.

regions.labelEs: SÍ QUE PONE A PRUEBA LOS LÍMITES DE LA FANTASÍA...

applications.explanationEn: Sí que adds strong confirmation before pone, the verb whose truth is being emphasized.
Pone a prueba supplies the testing expression, and los límites fills its role as the thing being tested.
Eso es is used as a complete reaction recognizing the preceding idea as the answer.

regions.labelEs: DIOS MÍO, ES LA ÚNICA EXPLICACIÓN: SOMOS OBJETOS EN ALGUNA FANTASÍA TRANSITORIA. ¡DESAPARECEREMOS EN CUANTO TERMINE!

applications.explanationEn: Dios mío is the complete emotional exclamation used before the speaker's realization.
The full verb keeps desaparecer and adds the future ending -emos for “we.”
Desapareceremos states the later future result; en cuanto introduces its future trigger, and termine uses the special form for an ending that has not happened yet.
Perder keeps its full dictionary form and adds -é for a future action by “I.”
Perder keeps its full dictionary form and adds -ás for a future action by informal singular “you.”

regions.labelEs: BIEN, NO ME VOY A IR SIN HACER RUIDO. VOY A QUEMAR ESTE PUTO MUNDO.

applications.explanationEn: Voy changes for the speaker, a links to the planned action, and ir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Sin introduces the action that is absent, and hacer remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
Hacer and ruido form the conventional Spanish pairing for making noise.
Voy changes for the speaker, a links to the planned action, and quemar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Quema is the positive informal command addressed to one person, formed from quemar.
Limpiar keeps its full dictionary form and adds -é for a future action by “I.”
